description: In June 1215, John Lackland affixed his seal to a charter imposed by his barons. A feudal text becomes, over the centuries, the symbol of the law above the king.

hero.hook: A cornered king signs. Eight centuries later, the whole world is still talking about it.

blocks.text: In June **1215**, in the **Runnymede** meadow, near London, the King of England **John Lackland** affixed his seal to the **Magna Carta**, the “Great Charter”. This is not a gesture of generosity. It's a standoff: the barons, great lords of the kingdom, want to break the royal arbitrary.
The text was born to avoid a civil war. Its immediate application fails. However, he gradually becomes the symbol of an explosive idea: even the king is under the law.

King since **1199**, Jean has one disaster after another. Facing the King of France , he suffered the . To reconquer his lands, he presses the : the king gives land in exchange for loyalty and military service, but John multiplies taxes, hostages and arbitrary fines. The customs that linked him to his vassals are shattered. [[Philip II Augustus]] [[The loss of Normandy (1204)]] [[The feudal system]]

The conflict with Pope  further isolates him. After the defeat of  (**1214**), where Philip Augustus defeated a coalition including England, the barons rebelled and took London. Jean no longer has a choice: negotiate, or lose the crown. [[Innocent III]] [[Bouvines]]
The nickname “Sans Terre” does not come from his French defeats. The last son of Henry II, he had simply received no prerogative at birth.

sections.title: John Lackland on the brink of the abyss

blocks.text: On **June 15, 1215**, the parties met at Runnymede. Influenced by the Archbishop of Canterbury , the document has **63 clauses**. Two of them change everything. The **clause 39**: no free man can be arrested without a judgment of his peers. The **clause 40**: the king can neither sell nor delay justice. [[Stephen Langton]]

blocks.caption: The Magna Carta of 1215, parchment that became a political myth.

blocks.text: It's not yet democracy. The charter speaks mainly to “free men”, not to serfs, peasants tied to the land. It is first of all a peace treaty between the king and his barons. But the idea is stated: power has written limits.

As early as August, John had the text annulled by the pope. The civil war resumes. The charter survives thanks to the death of the king in **1216**: the young **Henry III** reissues it to appease the kingdom. Confirmed again and again, it enters into English law.
There is no single original from 1215, but several copies sent to the counties. Only four survived.

In the 17th century, jurists like  brought it out against the absolutism of the Stuarts, these kings who wanted to govern without limits. A medieval parchment becomes the claimed ancestor of parliamentary freedoms. [[Edward Coke]]

sections.title: From a failure to a myth

blocks.text: British colonists take the charter to America. The Founding Fathers drew inspiration from it for the , the first amendments to the American Constitution. , the principle which prohibits arbitrary arrests, extends clause 39. In **1948**,  sees it as a “Great Charter” for all humanity. [[Bill of Rights]] [[Habeas corpus]] [[Eleanor Roosevelt]]
Today, only three clauses remain in force in England. Never mind. The Magna Carta counts less as a living law than as a symbol: no one is above the law.
Wrested from John Lackland in **1215**, the Magna Carta affirms that the king too is under the law. From a treaty between barons and king was born one of the founding myths of modern freedoms.
